To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the transcriptional response to starvation in the brain, liver, kidney, and small intestine is dominated by lipid metabolism and is controlled by nuclear receptors, whereas the skeletal muscle responds by increased proteolyses and is controlled by FOXOs.
1) The transcriptional response to starvation is complex and involves multiple organs.

the adaptive response to starvation is organ-specific, is controlled by common transcription factors that are different from the ones that are responsible for the adaptive response to nutrient excess, and is not restricted to the liver.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a comprehensive description and analysis of the interorgan coordination of the murine adaptive response to starvation.
the identification of the transcriptional regulators that control the interorgan metabolic adaptation to starvation, and with the elucidation of the mechanisms of this regulation.
the transcriptional control of the metabolic adaptation to fasting in different organs.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the adaptive response to fasting is organ-specific and is controlled at the transcriptional level.

the transcriptional response of the brain, liver, and kidney is directed to maintain energy homeostasis, whereas the small intestine is directed to maintain homeostasis of the intestinal epithelium, and muscle to prevent protein degradation and loss of muscle mass.
the adaptive response to fasting in the studied organs is a highly coordinated, organ-specific process, in which nuclear receptors are the key transcriptional regulators.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
fasting is a complex adaptive response that is coordinated by a large set of transcriptional regulators, and that the brain is the most protected organ.
the brain is the master organ of the organism, and the liver and kidney are the major players in the adaptive response.

the adaptive response to fasting in mice involves simultaneous and coordinated activation of metabolic pathways in different organs and is orchestrated by a set of transcriptional regulators that are common for most of the tissues.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the transcription factors that regulate the fasting-induced metabolic adaptations in the liver and muscle, and to a lesser degree in the kidney and intestine, have been known for decades.
the brain, the small intestine, the liver, and the muscle are not independent metabolic units, but are coordinated in a common metabolic network.
transcriptional regulation of metabolism in the brain, small intestine and muscle, and kidney, is organ-specific, whereas in the liver it is common to all of the studied organs.
